idiom_name: Jakarta Interceptors @AroundInvoke with an interceptor binding
implementation_notes: Java's declarative interception is a platform specification: an interceptor class binds to the target through an @InterceptorBinding annotation and exposes one @AroundInvoke method that takes the InvocationContext, records the audit event and calls ctx.proceed() to reach the target - the Jakarta EE tutorial names logging, auditing and profiling as the common uses. The container instantiates the interceptor with the target class lifetime and injects its dependencies, so the hand-written Interceptor/Dispatcher structure is replaced by container-managed interception; the price is that auditing only sees container-routed calls.
pitfalls: @AroundInvoke fires only for calls routed through a container-managed reference: self-invocation and calls on the raw instance are not audited.
Only one @AroundInvoke method per class is allowed, and binding order decides whether the audit record sees state before or after the authorization interceptor.
The interceptor shares the target's lifecycle and runs in the target's thread, security and transaction context - a slow or failing audit write therefore delays or aborts the business call.

variants.name: java.lang.reflect.Proxy with an InvocationHandler
variants.implementation_notes: Without a container, Proxy.newProxyInstance generates an interface implementation whose InvocationHandler.invoke runs the audit logic and dispatches with method.invoke(target, args) - the handler object is the Interceptor, and Method plus the argument array are the invocation context. This is the portable fallback for plain JDK code and libraries, at the cost of one reflective dispatch per call, interface-only targets, and the need to unwrap InvocationTargetException yourself.
pitfalls: Only interfaces can be proxied; a class-based target needs a hand-written decorator or a bytecode library such as ByteBuddy or CGLIB.
Target exceptions arrive wrapped in InvocationTargetException - unwrap with getCause() or the caller sees a different exception than the target threw.
Every call goes through reflection with boxed arguments, and proxies only cover calls that receive the proxy rather than the raw instance.
